extracted.intended_audience: graduate students / researchers in enumerative combinatorics and poset theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and records formal definitions, structural conditions, and key theorems about Eulerian posets, toric h-/g-polynomials, the cd-index, binomial posets and their reduced incidence algebra, generating-function identities, and the promotion/evacuation operators on linear extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of toric f and g polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: For an Eulerian poset P of rank n+1 the polynomials f(P,x) (degree n) and g(P,x) are defined inductively by: 1. f(1,x)=g(1,x)=1. 2. If rank(P)=n+1>0, write f(P,x)=h_0 + h_1 x + ... + h_n x^n and define g(P,x)=h_0 + (h_1 - h_0)x + (h_2 - h_1)x^2 + ... + (h_{⌊n/2⌋} - h_{⌊n/2⌋ - 1}) x^{⌊n/2⌋}. 3. If rank(P)=n+1>0 then f(P,x)= Σ_{Q ∈ P, Q ≠ ˆ1} g(Q,x) (x - 1)^{n-ρ(Q)} (equations (3.74)–(3.76)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inductive construction associates with each Eulerian poset two polynomials: the toric h-polynomial f(P,x) and the toric g-polynomial g(P,x). The coefficient sequence (h_0,...,h_n) is the toric h-vector. Use the specified recurrence (3.76) (sum over proper intervals [ˆ0,t]) when computing f(P,x) recursively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toric h-vector and toric g-vector
rubrics_metrics.description: The toric h-vector of P is the sequence (h_0, ..., h_n) of coefficients of f(P,x). The toric g-vector is the analogous sequence of coefficients of g(P,x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These vectors are the primary combinatorial invariants encoded by f(P,x) and g(P,x); computations of examples (e.g., boolean algebra B_n) illustrate typical values (for B_n, g_n = 1 and f_n = 1 + x + ... + x^{n-1}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Palindromicity of f(P,x) for Eulerian posets (Theorem 3.16.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is Eulerian of rank n+1 then f(P,x) = x^n f(P,1/x). Equivalently, if f(P,x)=Σ_{i=0}^n h_i x^i, then h_i = h_{n-i}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the symmetry (palindromic) property of the toric h-polynomial for Eulerian posets of rank n+1; equation (3.76) and the Möbius-inversion style proof in the text justify it. Use this to check computations: coefficients must read the same forwards and backwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic monomial and the ab-index Ψ_P(a,b)
rubrics_metrics.description: For S ⊆ [n-1] define the characteristic monomial u_S in noncommuting variables a,b by u_S = e_1 e_2 ... e_{n-1} where e_i = a if i ∉ S and e_i = b if i ∈ S. The ab-index Ψ_P(a,b) of a graded poset P of rank n is Ψ_P(a,b) = Σ_{S ⊆ [n-1]} β_P(S) u_S, a noncommutative generating function for the flag h-vector β_P(S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ψ_P encodes the flag h-vector in noncommuting variables; substitution identities (e.g., Ψ_P(a+b,b) = Σ α_P(S) u_S) relate different flag enumerators. This is the starting point for defining the cd-index for Eulerian posets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of the cd-index for Eulerian posets (Theorem 3.17.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is Eulerian of rank n then there exists a (noncommutative) polynomial Φ_P(c,d) in variables c and d such that Ψ_P(a,b) = Φ_P(a+b, ab+ba). The polynomial Φ_P(c,d) is called the cd-index of P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cd-index compresses all linear relations satisfied by the flag h-vector of Eulerian posets. The proof is by induction on rank using incidence-algebra manipulations; in computations replace c by (a+b) and d by (ab+ba) to recover Ψ_P. For face posets of regular cell complexes the example in the text shows how to compute Φ_P explicitly (e.g., Φ_P = c^3 + 3 c d + 2 d c for the given sphere decomposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneity and monomial count of the cd-index
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is Eulerian of rank n, then Φ_P(c,d) is homogeneous of degree n-1 when deg(c)=1 and deg(d)=2. The number of cd-monomials of degree n-1 equals the Fibonacci number F_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a dimension bound: the cd-index has at most F_n coefficients to specify, and these coefficients are linear combinations of the β_P(S) (and α_P(S)) depending only on n. Use the Fibonacci count to enumerate possible monomials when expanding Φ_P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary-symmetry corollary via cd-index
rubrics_metrics.description: From Ψ_P(a,b) = Φ_P(a+b, ab+ba) it follows immediately that Ψ_P(a,b) = Ψ_P(b,a) for Eulerian P, which is equivalent to the identity β_P(S) = β_P(S) (flag h-vector symmetry from Corollary 3.16.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cd-index formulation explains the classical β-symmetry: substituting (a,b) ↔ (b,a) corresponds to reversing words, and for Eulerian posets the ab-index is symmetric under that swap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicativity of cd-index under joins (equation (3.87))
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are Eulerian posets then the join P * Q is Eulerian and Φ_{P * Q}(c,d) = Φ_P(c,d) · Φ_Q(c,d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a way to construct Eulerian posets with prescribed cd-index coefficients via joins. Use the multiplicative property when building examples and to argue linear independence of cd-monomial coefficients by scaling factors in joins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear/affine dimension results for flag h-vectors (Theorem 3.17.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F_n denote the linear span of all flag h-vectors β_P of Eulerian posets of rank n. Then dim F_n = F_n (the Fibonacci number). Let G_n denote the affine span of all flag h-vectors; then dim G_n = F_n - 1 (there is one affine relation: the coefficient of c^{n-1} in Φ_P is 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dimension counts are tight; the proof uses joins of face lattices of polygons Q_m to produce cd-indices whose coefficients can be scaled independently, showing linear (and affine) independence of all coefficients except the enforced affine relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a binomial poset (three conditions, Definition 3.18.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poset P is called a binomial poset if (a) P is locally finite with ˆ0 and contains an infinite chain; (b) every interval [s,t] of P is graded (if ℓ(s,t)=n call it an n-interval); (c) for all n ∈ N any two n-intervals contain the same number B(n) of maximal chains. The sequence B(n) is the factorial function of P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three structural conditions rigidly control interval combinatorics and underpin the link between the combinatorics of P and families of generating functions of the form Σ f(n) x^n / B(n). When verifying binomial-poset status check all three conditions and compute B(n) from any n-interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical examples of binomial posets and factorial functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples given: (a) P = N with usual order (B(n)=1). (b) P = lattice of finite subsets (Boolean poset B) with B(n)=n!. (c) P = lattice of finite-dimensional subspaces over F_q (B(q)) with B(n) = (n)_q! (Eulerian generating denominators). (d) Products/Segre products (B_r = B * ... * B) give factorial functions B(n)=n!^r etc. (f) Veronese subposet P^(k) of rank-selected elements: factorial function B_k(n) = B(nk)/B(k)^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate why ordinary/exponential/Eulerian/etc. generating functions naturally appear: the denominator B(n) reflects the local factorial structure of the poset. Use these canonical models as test cases and to generate further constructions (joins, products, Veronese subposets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced incidence algebra R(P) and power-series isomorphism (Theorem 3.18.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a binomial poset P define R(P) = { f ∈ I(P) : f(s,t)=f(s',t') whenever ℓ(s,t)=ℓ(s',t') }. Then R(P) is a subalgebra of the incidence algebra I(P) and there is an algebra isomorphism φ : R(P) → C[[x]] given by φ(f) = Σ_{n≥0} f(n) x^n / B(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the conceptual linchpin: convolution in the incidence algebra corresponds to multiplication of power series with denominators B(n). Use φ to convert interval-functions into generating functions, perform algebra there, and convert back. The convolution formula (3.90) gives the multiplication rule in terms of the combinatorial numbers n choose i relative to B(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invertibility criterion in the reduced incidence algebra (Proposition 3.18.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ R(P) and f is invertible in the full incidence algebra I(P) (equivalently, the diagonal value f(t,t) is such that the constant term of φ(f) is invertible in C[[x]]), then the inverse f^{-1} also belongs to R(P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, invertibility can be checked via the power series φ(f): f has an inverse in R(P) iff φ(f) has an inverse in C[[x]]; then φ(f^{-1}) = φ(f)^{-1}. This allows using factorial-denominator generating-function algebra to determine interval-function inverses (e.g., Möbius function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Möbius-generating-function reciprocity (equation (3.91))
rubrics_metrics.description: For a binomial poset P with zeta ζ ∈ R(P) and Möbius µ ∈ R(P), their φ-images satisfy φ(µ) = φ(ζ)^{-1}. Thus the generating function Σ µ(n) x^n / B(n) is the multiplicative inverse of Σ ζ(n) x^n / B(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to compute µ(n) for canonical examples by taking reciprocals of known ζ-series. Examples provided: for P = N and P = B (boolean), the Möbius generating series reduce to simple closed forms (matching classical Pólya/PIE identities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating-function identity for rank-selected Möbius functions (Lemma 3.19.1)
rubrics_metrics.description:
Let S ⊆ N and µ_S(n) be the Möbius function of the S-rank-selected subposet of any n-interval. Then the generating functions satisfy (equation (3.94)):
  Σ_{n≥0} µ_S(n) x^n / B(n) = (Σ_{n≥0} χ(n) x^n / B(n))^{-1} * Σ_{n≥0} (something...)  (text gives precise rearrangement deriving from the recurrence for µ), where χ(n)=1 if n=0 or n ∈ S and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma reduces computation of rank-selected Möbius series to algebraic manipulations in the reduced incidence algebra; the proof uses the defining Möbius recurrence and the combinatorial coefficients B(n)/(B(i) B(n-i)). Apply it to special S to get closed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed form for µ_S when S = kP via Veronese subposet (Lemma 3.19.2 and Corollary 3.19.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If k ∈ P and S = kP = {kn : n ∈ P}, then the generating function 1 + Σ_{n≥1} µ_S(n) x^n / B(n) has a simple closed form obtained by relating µ_S to the Möbius function of the Veronese subposet P^(k) whose factorial function is B_k(n) = B(kn)/B(k)^n (equation (3.95)): 1 + Σ µ_S(n) x^n / B(n) = 1 / (1 - x^k substituted appropriately using B(k)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses P^(k) and the φ-isomorphism: compute φ(µ^{(k)}) = 1 / (1 - ...) and substitute to get the explicit series for µ_S. This yields many elegant generating-function identities when P is a canonical binomial poset (e.g., B(q)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutation-enumeration corollaries via rank-selection (Proposition 3.19.4 and equations (3.97)–(3.100))
rubrics_metrics.description: For P = B(q) and S = kP the q-weighted count f_{n,k}(q) of permutations in S_n whose descent set lies in S satisfies a tidy generating-function identity (equation (3.97)): Σ_{n≥1} ( (n-1)/k floor ) f_{n,k}(q) x^n / (n)! = (Σ_{n≥1} µ_S(n) x^n/(n)!) · (1/(1 - x^{k}/(kn)!))^{-1} (text gives exact form). Specializing k=2, q=1 recovers the classical alternating-permutation generating function Σ E_n x^n/n! = sec x + tan x (equation (3.100)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identities explain why certain permutation statistics (e.g., alternating permutations) have exceptionally simple exponential-type generating functions: they arise from Möbius/Veronese manipulations in binomial-poset algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of promotion ∂ on linear extensions (promotion operator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a linear extension f of a p-element poset P (labels 1..p), promotion ∂: remove label 1 from its element t_1, then repeatedly 'slide' the smallest label among the elements covering the current vertex down into the previous vertex along a chain t_1 ⋖ t_2 ⋖ ... until reaching a maximal element t_k; place label p+1 at t_k, then subtract 1 from every label to obtain the new linear extension f ∂. The chain t_1⋖...⋖t_k is the promotion chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit combinatorial algorithm. Implementation must follow the sliding rule precisely (always choose the covering element with smallest label to slide). ∂ is a bijection on the set of linear extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual promotion and evacuation operations (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dual promotion ∂* is defined analogously by removing the largest label and sliding labels upward. Evacuation ǫ is defined by iterating promotion and 'freezing' the largest labels: compute f ∂, freeze the top label p in place, restrict to remaining elements and apply ∂, freeze p-1, and so on until all labels are frozen; the resulting labeling is f ǫ. Dual evacuation ǫ* defined analogously from the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evacuation is obtained by a sequence of promotions on successively smaller subposets; one may think of evacuation as 'promote repeatedly and freeze' until all labels are fixed. Careful bookkeeping of frozen labels is required in implementations or proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic properties of promotion and evacuation (Theorem 3.20.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let P have p elements. The operators ∂, ǫ, ǫ* satisfy: (a) evacuation is an involution: ǫ^2 = identity. (b) ∂^p = ǫ ǫ*. (c) ∂ ǫ = ǫ ∂^{-1}. Equivalently, the group generated by ǫ and ǫ* is (possibly degenerate) dihedral; their relations describe the cycle structure of ∂^p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These structural relations are foundational in the combinatorial/algebraic study of promotion/evacuation; they let one deduce global permutation-group properties from the local sliding rules. Use (a)-(c) when deriving symmetry or order properties of these maps on linear extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coxeter-like algebraic framework for proofs (relations (3.101) and Lemma 3.20.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a group G generated by τ_1,...,τ_{p-1} with relations τ_i^2=1 and τ_i τ_j = τ_j τ_i when |i-j|>1 (a subset of symmetric-group Coxeter relations). Define δ_j = τ_1 τ_2 ... τ_j, γ_j = δ_j δ_{j-1} and γ_j^* = τ_j τ_{j-1} ... τ_1. Lemma 3.20.2 asserts identities among these elements (e.g., γ_j^2 = (γ_j^*)^2 = 1, δ_{j+1} δ_j = γ_j γ_j^*, δ_j γ_j = γ_j δ_j^{-1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebraic setup translates the combinatorial promotion/evacuation operations into group-element identities and supports the proofs of Theorem 3.20.1 via algebraic manipulations. When proving properties, map combinatorial moves to these generators and use the stated relations.
